utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I'd like to deal briefly with a -- let me see. No, I'll leave that until after we've heard the next witness. Are there any preliminaries to be raised? Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: -- morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Ms. Hasan, you want to -- because we ended yesterday with a submission you made on -- on two different statements. Has that any follow-up?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, we still have concerns about the process involved, and my understanding was that was going to be addressed this morning, before the appearance of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any other matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Then the Chamber would like to be informed in detail about the two statements. You said yesterday, Ms. Hasan, that they were signed on the same date. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That's correct. It appears to me that it's the same witness acknowledgment or confirmation that is appended to both versions of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, could you clarify what happened? And in order to avoid any confusion, the Chamber is aware that there are two versions of the statement. The one is -- consists of 27 paragraphs; the other one consists of 25 paragraphs. So, in order to avoid any confusion, could you always refer to which one, the 27 or the 25 version, you are dealing with. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. I will try to explain the confusion that arose in connection with this witness. The 25-paragraph statement is longer, although it has less paragraphs, and it was part of a -- our 92 ter package offered with this witness, actually, coming witness. The witness signed that statement, and it's obvious from the signature page where it -- it says that he signed a statement that has nine pages. And that's that -- actually, this 25-paragraph statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But could you please -- we see that, that it was -- well, at least there is a signature on the statement, 2nd of May, and then we also see the numbering of those pages may require some additional explanation as well. It moves from 18 to 2, 3, 4, 5, 26, which is a rather strange order. But -- okay. Could you tell us exactly chronologically what happened. The witness was interviewed when?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As it says here, he was interviewed in March and April 2013, and in February 2014.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That -- what happened then. He was interviewed. When was his statement put on paper?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: His statement was put on paper after that, but, as you know, it wasn't signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I know that. But when was it put on paper? Immediately after the last day. That's in February. Or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. How did it then happen that two versions were drafted?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you could see, several people spoke to this person but not at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I know that the last conversation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we do not know whether they were all there during all these interviews or not because that information is not provided here. So it could well be that all three have been present during all the four days, but it's also possible that not all of them attended all the four days. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not all of them, I think, attended all four days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, that's what you think. Yes, okay. So interviewed, you don't know when it was put on paper. How did it happen that two versions were drafted?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Two people worked at the same time parallelly -- parallel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- and they produced two statements. The longer statement, 25-paragraph statement, was offered through 92 ter motion but we had the shorter one in our system as well, of course. Essentially, there is -- I think there is nothing different in those statements, only probably in different words. They even compared each other's statements, that's compilation, actually. They mixed their work. But our Case Manager was back home when we had to file the -- the signatures. From the field, we got only two pages to expedite things. We got only first and the last page in e-mail, and we forwarded that to the Prosecution so they have only this first and last page as we got in the e-mail. Since our Case Manager was not here, somebody else had to do his job and did it wrongly, attached signatures to the shorter statement, and then it was sent as allegedly and it was not checked that it should be with the statement of nine pages, not with the statement of five pages. And that's what created all the confusion. So the witness, and you will probably ask him, the witness signed the statement, nine-page statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: When did the witness sign the -- which statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He signed nine-page statement on the -- here it says 10th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I can see that. But when did he sign it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have witness here. Maybe it's better to ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but, Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you should know. You should know whether the witness signed the statement on the day on which he is said to have signed it under present circumstances. Under normal circumstances I would agree with you that you accept that it was signed on the date as mentioned, but when there are two versions, when the signature apparently can be attached to another statement, then under those circumstances, you, as lead counsel, should know exactly what happened. So you say: I do not know whether it really was signed on the 10th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't know where it was signed?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know it was signed in Sarajevo. They had to go into the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you do not know what was then presented to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Nine-page statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nine-page statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked the statement yesterday while on the phone with Ms. Hasan, I asked the witness, "Which statement was presented to you," and he told me that it was nine-page. I put number nine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask why wasn't this signed statement with the date of 10th April attached to the 92 ter motion? There was, as we see it, only an unsigned version of the statement, although you had already the signed -- the signature of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That -- that's why it creates confusion on my part as well. I think that it's not signed on this date. Otherwise we would attach. Obviously they had to go into the field after 5th of May, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then if he signed on the -- after the 5th of May --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could be 10th of May. I really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But if it says that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I tried --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it says that it was signed on the 10th of April, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now -- now my colleague -- sorry. My colleague Ivetic is telling me that we got it on the 12th of May, so it must be 10th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But if you had to send back someone early May to get a signature, then, to say the least, one is surprised to find a signature dated the 10th of April. We'll ask the witness about it, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's why we think that's the best not go with the statements and that's why we propose to have this witness viva voce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that doesn't resolve the whole of the problem. Especially not the last portion of the problem I hinted at; that is that there may be a falsity in the dates of signature, and if this happens here, of course, the Chamber, as always, until now, relied on your professionality, but if these kind of things happen and if just signatures are attached to statements one version, another version, one working on it, another person working on it, comparing, but nevertheless, they're all the same but they're not the same, they're different, that's something that is of great concern to the Chamber. That's also the reason why even if the witness testifies viva voce, that we, nevertheless, want this to be sorted out in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I -- I had a strange question, Your Honour, last night. One of the investigators in the field, from the field, asked me, should I have date of the -- when we took the statement or the date when he is really signing. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that is a question, then please do something about the training of your persons --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I did explain, and it was last night so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The concern only grows at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I think that he hasn't started giving the statements for signatures yet. So he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we do not know that. And we do not know who you are talking about. Let's -- Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say that earlier I had this concern and it is growing in my mind, the disconnection between the signature page and the statement. I'm going to ask the Chamber to give an instruction that, from this point forward, the statements and the signature page, the signatures should appear after the last paragraph in the statement and not be some separate document. I think that would alleviate some of the issues that are coming to the fore now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The statements are -- some of the statements are already sent, I think, to the field and for the translation at the same time, and I think that we have the same pattern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, that's, of course, also a lack of professionality. If I receive a draft which I'm supposed to sign, if I have the signature page separate, I'll send my staff back and insist on having part of the decision on the page I sign. That's simple, professional behaviour, and I do understand that it's -- now, and if you deviate from that, that's one. But if you then attach the statement to -- the signature page to a statement to which it doesn't belong, then the basis for this professional rule becomes the more clearer. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I also ask that Mr. Lukic have the witness initial and date each page of the statement since that would remove any kind of confusion when it was reviewed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we'll see how this develops because we do understand from Mr. Lukic that some statements are signed already. We'll later consider how to deal with those. At least for any new statement, Mr. Lukic, this would be the rule: No separate signature pages and every page of the statement to be signed or as initialled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if the Defence is ready to call its next witness, Mr. Batinic, could he be escorted into the courtroom. The Chamber may wish to clarify the issue with the witness first, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Batinic. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. Could you please make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Batinic. Please be seated. Mr. Batinic, before you'll be examined by the Defence, there are a few questions about a statement you've given to Defence counsel. Could I have 1D01604 on the screen. Mr. Batinic, do you see the cover page of this statement; and do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we go to the last page of the same document. Mr. Batinic, on this last page, do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you see the date below it? And could you tell us whether you wrote that date or whether you -- someone else did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, did you write this down on the 10th of April, as it says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I wrote this on the 10th of April, in the presence of the gentleman from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you tell us exactly then where you were when you signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] East Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With whom were you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was with Mr. Dundjer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With Mr. Dundjer alone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, this was not one of the dates on which you were interviewed. Could you tell us how you came to the place in East Sarajevo where you signed this statement, this page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Dundjer came and called me to come. There were other witnesses signing papers. He was in a hurry, under some sort of pressure. Many people had to do this paperwork. Those were orders from The Hague, as I was told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, how much time did you take to sign? Was it a matter of minutes, was it half an hour? Did you have to wait very long? Could you describe in detail what happened on that day. First of all, who invited you? Was it done by telephone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was a telephone call. I had been invited before to be there in East Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's now focus on the day when you went there for your signature. You received a call. From whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I got a telephone call from Belgrade, telling me that Mr. Dundjer would be there on that day and that I should also come to sign this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. What was the place where you would meet him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the office of the administration for co-operation with The Hague, as far as I could see. And other witnesses beside me had come. But I reviewed my document and said some corrections were needed because some things did not really fit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it step by step. You received a phone call. How many days before you were supposed to go to that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was the day before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Had you received at that time already a written version of the statement drafted on the basis of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I did not receive the statement. I saw it at the Office for Co-operation with The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You went to the office. Could you tell us how many witnesses or persons you considered to have come for the same purpose were there, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not everybody came at the same time. There was a number of people, and, for a while, I sat in a cafe waiting. I didn't want to interfere with the lawyer's job. But when I was there, there were two more people. Then I left. Other people were coming. After that, I took them to Pale, I mean, Mr. Dundjer. And some people signed their statements in Pale. Because Mr. Dundjer was very pressed for time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- let's take it again step by step. You came. What happened exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Various witnesses came to the office. They were given their statements, and they would review them and sign them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, just you yourself, you received your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I reviewed my statement, and I said corrections are needed because some dates do not correspond. However, Mr. Dundjer said: Sign it, please. You will make the corrections in The Hague. Because I could see he was pressed for time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you signed the statement, though you had indicated that corrections were needed but they were not made yet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time did you get to review your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received a copy of the statement that I didn't sign. I signed one copy and gave it to Mr. Dundjer, and I saved one copy for me, so I had practically months to review it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But at the moment when you signed it, you received it, how much time elapsed between the moment you got the statement in your hands until you signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when I signed the original statement, I received a copy that I took home. And that signed statement was given to Mr. Dundjer. They were identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, do I understand that the corrections you thought would be necessary, that you only detected them after you had signed, or did you immediately say: It's not accurate. It needs to be corrected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. I said it immediately. I said immediately: There are mistakes in names and dates, et cetera. Mr. Dundjer said: It's not a problem. You will make these corrections together with lawyer Lukic. He was simply under pressure for those documents to be filed as soon as possible. Those were orders in The Hague. And he was then dealing with 20 different witnesses, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. 20 witnesses is the total number of people you saw were around at any point in time? Is that how I have to understand it? Or is it that you were told that there were 20? Or how did you come to the number of 20?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll explain. That morning when I arrived, perhaps around 9.30, I know that some people had already passed through that office and signed their statements. There were some people around at that moment when I was in a cafe. Other people were coming and going, and then we left for Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can I stop you there first. How did you know that others had come all ready and had already signed? Had they left? And if so, how did you know that they had been there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know. The secretary was there. And I heard from her that some people had already signed their statements, before me. And then later, I drove Mr. Dundjer to Pale where there were some more people signing statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll come to that in a second. So you got the statement. You reviewed it, said that there were inaccuracies, and you were invited nevertheless to sign. Now, how much time did you take to read through it up till the moment that you were urged to sign despite inaccuracies? Was it ten minutes? Was it half an hour? Was it an hour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly how many minutes, but I did review the whole statement in detail and indicated which corrections needed to be made. And twice I said: I don't want to sign this. It's not correct. And he responded: Go on, sign it. Those are orders from The Hague. You will correct it on the ground with Mr. Lukic. So then I signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. And then you signed. You do not know exactly how much time you needed for that. Okay. And then you said you went to Pale with Mr. Dundjer. Why did you go to Pale? Did he ask you or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said: I'll give you a lift to make it shorter, because there are more people to sign their statements, and I took them to Pale because I know the place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How many people were in your car? Was there just Mr. Dundjer or were there others and what was their function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only Mr. Dundjer. Two or three more people came to Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And were they persons who had also signed or were they just people you knew or what the other three people -- or do you mean the three people came to Pale for signing their statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. They signed their statements in Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they were not your car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember who these three were by name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember one name, Mr. Cvoro, who had already testified by now. The other two I don't remember. I remember only Mr. Cvoro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You met him here in The Hague? You met him in Pale and not in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I met him in Pale, not The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, were you present when these three persons in Pale signed their statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was there. I know the two of them signed. As for the third one, I went out into the street to have a smoke, so I didn't see the third man actually signing, but I'm sure he did. And then I went back to East Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you also present when they reviewed their statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I remember two of them who signed before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How long did they take for reading the statement before they signed? If you remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember they signed very quickly. They had already made their statements before somewhere else. I think they just gave it a quick glance and signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did they make any comments in relation to the content of their statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there was no comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After that, you returned home, if I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I took Mr. Dundjer back to the hotel where he was staying, which is in East Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, there is another version of your statement. I don't know whether you're aware of that. That is -- could we have a look at 65 ter 1D07028.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the meantime, I would like to ask one question. Sir, we saw -- at the moment, we still see on the screen the date of 10th of April, 2014. Did you really sign it on that day or one month later, on the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see the date, 10 April. Whether it's true that I really signed on 10 May, I really don't know. I don't know whether it was a month ago or two months ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How did you -- the date, did you look at your watch? How did you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How did you -- I mean, you said you have -- was it -- were you told to say the date is the 10th of April or -- or did you verify yourself whether it was the 10th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't wear a watch, and I didn't check. I just asked around, what's the date, and I was told 10 April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But do you know whether any month is April or May even if you don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I signed it on the 10th of April. Now I see that it's -- says 10 May. I didn't pay attention. These are formalities to me. I signed because it was my statement. And I asked around: What's the date today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, you said just now: "Now I see that it's -- that it says 10 May." Where do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see anywhere. I see 10 April, so it's the month of April. Now I see where the mistake lies. At that time I wasn't paying attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if it really happened on the 10th of May and the document says 10 April, then it's a mistake. But as for the statement itself, I signed it. This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand that. But I'm not saying that it was on the 10th of May. I'm just asking you: Was it from today one month ago or two months ago, in your memory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you should really ask Mr. Dundjer. I really don't remember the date. Time passes very quickly for me. I don't pay attention to dates. Only when I see it in my agenda, when I am dealing with journalists, when I'm dealing with tourism, et cetera, when I have commitments, but I don't pay attention to dates otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about dates but about months. Was it one month ago or two months ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm really not sure. It could have been either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first go to -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How many statements in total did you sign?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I signed this statement. Whether maybe I signed something last year at the first confrontation, maybe. But it would have been more than a year ago. But I remember signing this statement clearly. It was nine pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you just answer me clearly. How many statements do you remember signing? Don't tell me a story. Say two, three, four, one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I signed one statement. That's what I know for sure. It's this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The reason I'm asking you this question is this. Today, at page 11 of the transcript, lines 18 to 23, you said the following. Line 21 you were being asked by Judge Orie: "Had you received at that time already a written version of the statement drafted on the basis of," and then there was an overlap. Your answer was: "No, no. I did not receive a statement. I saw it at the Office for Co-operation with The Hague Tribunal." Just hold that. At page 12, from -- page 12, line 24, to page 13, line 7, the following is recorded: "I received a copy of the statement that I did not sign. I signed one copy and gave it to Mr. Dundjer and I saved one copy for me, so I had practically months to review it." Now, first you said you did not have -- receive any statement. You saw it at the office administration where were told to sign. Now you say you had practically months to review it. Can -- how do you explain the difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll repeat once again. The statement that I signed at the office is the same as the copy of the statement that I took home. I'll come back to that. It's that signed statement. That statement was in my apartment, and I reviewed. However, since Mr. Dundjer had said that Mr. Lukic would be there to make the corrections, I didn't go into any further detail. I just let him know that corrections needed to be made. So I signed the statement in a rush because, as I was told, The Hague Tribunal ordered that all the statements had to be signed. The man was really in a hurry, dealing with a lot of people. So I signed the statement after telling him many times that I didn't want to sign it because it's not entirely correct, but after his insistence, I finally signed it, nevertheless, to -- to simply make his life easier because he was really in big trouble. I'm talking about Veljko Dundjer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Let me clarify this briefly. When you said: "... so I had practically months to review it," did you mean from the moment you signed it up to now, here in The Hague? Do you mean this time-period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the signing, that's this period that I mean, I had the statement at my home for a month, maybe two, and I had already said after glancing through it that corrections needed to be made, and -- I had no further communication with people from Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand that. I just wanted to clarify when you -- when you are talking about the months to review it, it was the month or two months after the signature?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll take it there --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will take it there step by step again. There were two copies. One you retained; the other one was signed, and you left it behind. Now, you had, you said, a month - at the same time it could be one month or two months - to review it. What did you then -- how did you communicate the details of the changes you wanted to be made? Did you wait until you arrived in The Hague? Did you -- were you in touch with Belgrade? What happened? Tell us exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The most precise answer is that I was waiting for Mr. Lukic to make these corrections in The Hague. Because I'm not good at handling computers, it would have taken a lot of time for me to do it back there. I thought we would do it here, and that's what I had arranged with Mr. Dundjer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So you didn't do anything until you arrived in The Hague. Now, you arrived in The Hague. What then happened? You sat together with Mr. Lukic or with someone else? With whom did you sit together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With Mr. Lukic. I was sitting with him and making these corrections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, your statement, which we looked at a minute ago, was 27 paragraphs. Could we have on the screen page 5 in the original. You see that it has 27 paragraphs. Now, did you ever see a new version of --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I hesitate to interrupt, Mr. President. But I believe that this version we're looking at now is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, is the one --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken is the second version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's the second version. Okay. Then I -- I apologise. The one who is now before you is 27 paragraphs; whereas the previous one was 25 paragraphs. Now, can you explain exactly what did you tell Mr. Lukic what had to be changed? Did he come up with a proposal, or did you propose to him what had to be changed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. I didn't make any proposals to him and he didn't make any proposals to me. I just said these are the corrections that should be made. And these are the corrections that were made because I know, on the basis of the document, what is correct and what is not correct and what I said and what is not in line with the document. Now, how this happened, how these paragraphs happened, I really don't know. I just know that I was sitting with Mr. Lukic so that we could make the corrections in this nine-page document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now what changes were made, then, exactly? I -- we see that there's a one -- on the cover page, there is a handwritten correction but that's about your name. What else was then changed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember very well the date was 1994 and it was supposed to be 1992 or 1993. So it's these minor points, these nuances. The essence was not the change. For example, I have this example. It says Novitski [phoen] instead of Olivier Mrowicki, things like that. Names, years, that's the kind of mistake that was made, so it changes the entire context. I think that most of the mistakes were of a technical nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you indicated that that had to be changed. Did you then see a new copy in which the changes were made or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, precisely I have that copy, so with Mr. Lukic, the one that I made with him, and I looked at it and it was all correct. So I got that printed out, the corrections that we had made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there was a new version compared to the one you signed in Sarajevo, in which names, dates, years were changed. Was there anything else that had changed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Corrections of names, corrections of years, I don't know what else was changed. Now how come 25, I don't know. I mean, the first version was 27. Now, what it was that was abbreviated, I don't know. Because of time and these proceedings, I don't know. I just stuck to the things that I know, saying: This name is not correct, this year is not correct, the context is not the one that is being discussed. Those were my observations made to Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then a new version was presented to you in which the changes were incorporated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have that version. I think it's in my hotel room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And was that signed by you in any way or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, I didn't sign it. It's a correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And when was it that you sat together and that you made these --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the day when I saw Mr. Lukic. That was that Monday, since I flew in on Sunday. So we started -- I mean, saw each other every day. I think the correction was made on the first day. That would be Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when did you then receive the new copy, the new version you say you have in your hotel room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lukic printed it out for me immediately so I had it there in front of me. It was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So at the very moment that you made these corrections, they were put in the computer and immediately a printout was made on the basis of your corrections. Would you still have that corrected version in your hotel room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should. I should have it. If it's in the hotel room, that's where it is. It can be nowhere else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you be willing to provide that changed version to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be pleased to do that. And I will take the statement, if it is there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if you say you left it in your hotel room, how could it not be there anymore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should be there. I have a few statements here. These are questions, actually. If it's not in the hotel room, then Mr. Lukic has it. I know that he printed it out for me, so maybe it's in his office. In my hotel room, I have quite a few papers, so I looked at it after he printed it out for me. I really don't know. Maybe I took it to the hotel room. I'll take a look. But it certainly does exist. I finished these corrections with Mr. Lukic. I reviewed the document. There was no need for me to sign it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now you have a few papers in front of you. You say: "These are questions." Could you explain to us what the papers are that you were just pulling out of your pocket. Questions written down by whom and for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be very happy to answer that question to you. Because of these problems concerning statements, yesterday Mr. Lukic said: Then we're going to do this live, that is to say, without these signed statements. So our time is very brief, so this is a reminder for you to be reminded of what the questions are going to be. So that is what I have here. It is simply as a reminder for me to see how the trial will go. Time has been shortened so we simply won't be able to go through the statements, I guess the Court does not accept them, so these are the questions and they are right here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it just questions or is there more on these pieces of paper? Is there also hints to answers or any other notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's simply his questions. I have them here, and then I made some notes, simply for the sake of my memory, so that I could remember the exact things that happened. I can give this to you. These are the questions. So that is how he explained the process to me, that it would be live. There are some problems with statements. They do not overlap. There are corrections so we'll have to deal with it this way, unfortunately. But these are the questions that will be put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you jotted down reminders for the answers to be given to those questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely. Precisely. Just to have it in front of me. I mean, well, of course, you can put all the questions you like, Your Honour. I am ready to answer all the questions you may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No doubt about that, Witness. Just, did you jot down those reminders for answers to be given in the presence of Mr. Lukic, or did you do it after he had left, or -- how did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Last night. I sat down, simply trying to remember. It was a reminder for me personally. You see, I'm a historian by training, that's my profession, so chronology is important for me. And this a court, an exceptional court, and I have to give expectational answers and it's a honour for me to do so. That you ask me to come, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You -- a minute ago, you offered that we could have a look at the papers you just had. We gladly accept that offer. So if you could provide it to the usher, then we may have a look at it and may share that with the parties. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can bring it to you myself. The gentleman doesn't have to make an effort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, that's how it works in this courtroom. We will take a break. Witness, we'll take a break. And we'll resume at 11.00. You may follow the usher. And hopefully soon we'll start with your examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Met plezier, Meneer Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Understood. For the interpreters: With pleasure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume for a moment without the witness. The Chamber received copies of the papers -- has received the original of the paper the witness had before him which he said were questions and his own annotations as reminders for answering those questions. Apart from that, it seems that the witness also has given us one page which seems to be VWS guidance or information for a witness; at least that's what we thought it most likely would be. Then we have not sought, up till this moment, any translation of the document, including the handwriting of the witness. But it would be unfair to say that we do not have a -- a bit of an impression of some subjects that are dealt with in those questions, if only on the basis of the titles. Mr. Lukic, the Chamber would like to know whether you have -- because we are not talking about two versions at this moment anymore, but about three versions of a statement. Do you have a copy of the statement which was produced last Monday, as the witness said, on the basis of his comments and corrections to the statement he had signed earlier? He had seen earlier, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I have with me, Your Honour, is information report I sent to the Prosecution with those corrections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, we did receive the information report on the -- Tuesday evening, the 10th. It is has been uploaded under 65 ter 30802.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that one of the parties will use that later or will put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You'll see three dates were corrected and one name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that corresponds very much with what the witness told us, the type of -- yes. Then it's still a puzzle how the two versions, the 25-paragraph and the 27-paragraph, how they could be produced. We have not looked at it in detail at this moment, but, of course, by comparing them, you could ask yourself whether they were produced independently, where you would expect a totally different text, or whether they are in one way or another related, the one to the other --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They are related. But this shorter version with more paragraphs is -- is written by another team member who was trying, reading the first, the longer one, not -- not being able to understand everything, trying to cut it down and make it more understandable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which suggests that the content of the new version could not be any different, at least could not add anything, because that person apparently had not spoken to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The person did speak with the witness. So he had his own notes. So it's some kind of compilation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us who that was Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sasa Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was Sasa Lukic who made a new version. And the first version was drafted by --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dundjer Milenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By Dundjer Milenko. Yes. Further, I would give you an opportunity to comment on what the witness said about signing statements. Changes will be made later in The Hague, sign now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah. I had -- I screamed at my investigators in the field when I heard about it because I told them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did you hear about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When the witnesses -- when this witness complained here that he was told that the changes would be made in The Hague. I -- I was trying to explain to the investigators that then it's too late. The changes have to be done before, in advance, to give them to the Prosecution if there are any changes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the first thing you would have had to do was to inform the Chamber that signatures were requested from witnesses where they did not yet agree with the statements. That was your duty to do first of anything else, even before starting screaming to your team members. I leave it to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one observation on the record. The Witness Batinic told us that he was, together with Witness Cvoro at Pale and signing statements. I just looked into the statement of Witness Cvoro, this is D492, and this is dated 10th of May, 2014. I just want to put that on the record because we had that discussion about the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it is not only about Witness Cvoro but all the other statements apparently were signed on the 10th of May. We have seen many of those dates, so apparently there has been -- most likely there has been a mistake in the date. Ms. Hasan, I would like to give you an opportunity as well to briefly comment on what we've heard until now, to see whether we can proceed or whether there's anything else we should do at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. There are still some areas for clarification. I can do that during the cross-examination. However, there are some matters that perhaps Mr. Lukic can clarify. For instance, as I understand it now, Milenko Dundjer takes a first statement from the witness. At some later time - and we don't know when - Sasa Lukic sees the witness, receiving information. I don't know if it's the same information from the witness, additional information. At some point the Defence has received more information for this witness because in the second version of the statement, while it is true that there are some language changes, some abbreviations, some paragraphs are cut, there are additions to the statement. So there was clearly a point in time where more information was given to this witness which, to me, it's not clear when the Defence was aware of that new information because we only received the proofing note on the 10th of June, which was two days ago. I don't know when Sasa Lukic met with this witness and compiled this second version, which we didn't see until yesterday. Second, in the proofing note, it provides that the witness reviewed his statement which is 65 ter 1D1604. This is the second statement, second version. As far as I understood from the witness, this was not the statement that he reviewed. And the clarifications that are made in this proofing note are to the second version of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The second version being the short one. The 25-paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No, it would be the long -- the 27-paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the 27-paragraph is -- let me check now, and let's put that clear forever. The -- let me have a look. The 27-paragraph is the paragraph [sic] which contains six pages and is wrongly attached to the signatures.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the witness has reviewed the longer one, which is 25 paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that's the one he reviewed when signing. And that is the one which was -- not the one uploaded into e-court but --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Correct. Not the one uploaded into e-court but apparently the one that was discussed during the proofing session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you'd say that in this comedy of errors, they put the wrong -- or tragedy of errors, I do not know how to say, but that they put the wrong statement to the witness, at least it's recorded that they put the wrong statement to the witness to review. Well, we hear his testimony anyway viva voce, questions are known already --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can -- I can clarify a bit this confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since I was not aware that there were two statements, I gave the witness his statement. He actually brought it with him, the statement which he was given in the field. And since I had 1D1604 uploaded as his statement, he was working with his statement when he was talking about the dates, I was working with the statement that was uploaded. So that's why being unaware of the existence of the -- the other statement, that's why I made the proofing note according to the statement I had and I worked with but he worked with his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I haven't seen the proofing note so I do not know whether references to paragraphs would confirm or would --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can send Your Honours the proofing note as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Anything else at this moment, Ms. Hasan, you would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes. If we can get clarification as to who appended the declaration that was filed with the 92 ter package to the new statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who changed the -- Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Declaration was changed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But who attached the wrong statement to the first and last signature pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic did it. Since our case manager was not here. His --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: His wife, our case manager's wife was expecting at that time. He [sic] gave a birth so he was home for a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Everything fine with the baby?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Everything's fine with the baby.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the mother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and the mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I dumped this task to Mr. Ivetic who was not obviously privy with everything that should be done, but he could not say no because we had to do it. And it was done wrongly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now a lot of matters have been clarified, not to say that some concerns remain. But, Ms. Hasan, anything else?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I believe I can address the rest of the matters during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, just as the witness is being brought in, my understanding is that the witness speaks English very well, so should there be any matters that the witness should not hear, it's probably best that he leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's try to avoid it, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just want to say it's my fifth question to ask him which languages is he speaking so it would be clarified as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- at the beginning. He speaks Dutch as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I said before, we have not sought it to be interpreted for us. So it's still a surprise what the questions will be. But the question is superfluous now since both parties agree on the witness mastering the English language. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, at this moment no further questions about statements or versions or whatever. You'll now be examined on the substance of the matter by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Batinic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Good morning to you too. How are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're not here to put questions to anybody, not even to ask me how I am. I am the one who will be putting all the questions.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a little joke to break the ice.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Of course, it's in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us for the record what is your name.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: My name is Milorad Batinic. And more people know me as Lola, which is my nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about your education, can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: I have a university degree. I am a history teacher. However, I have not been teaching for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you live before the war?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: I lived in Blazuj, about 15 kilometres away from the centre of Sarajevo, near Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you to make a small pause between question and answer and answer and question, so as to avoid overlapping speakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We did say that we should make little pauses. You can look at the screen and you will see when the interpretation of your words, or mine, stops. What languages do you speak, Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: I speak English and I'm fluent in Dutch.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the nationality of your wife?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: My wife is of Dutch origin. She's a Dutch citizen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you work before the war?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: My last employment was at Vrace, which is a memorial park. I worked there as a curator.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how long did you go to work?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Until mid-April. The war had already started but we could still go to work. One day we could no longer enter the city. There were barricades, there was shelling, so it was dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please wait for the questions to be interpreted. What about your parents? Where did they reside?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: My parents lived in Sarajevo, on the main street in the very centre of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the health of your parents?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: My father is now 90, but my mother was not -- was not in good health, and she died as a refugee in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did your mother move about at the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: She was wheelchair-bound because she had a leg amputated. With the help of my father and with our help, she could move about, but only with our help.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you try to take your parents out of the city?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did try desperately to take them out of the city. Owing to my friend who's a Muslim - currently this is Bosniak nationality - after the third attempt, he managed to bring them to the separation line. And to this very day I am grateful to him for having done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you help anybody else to move out of Sarajevo and when was that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very well. During the war, in 1993, in the month of December, I worked with the UNMO section of UNPROFOR. With the help of a UN observer, I helped somebody to get out of the occupied part of the city, and I also helped a friend of my wife's to go to the Serbian part of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was it who prevented civilians from leaving the city?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: It was the Bosnian government, i.e., the Muslim authorities. That's what we called them at the time. They were the ones who put obstacles before the people. After they obtained many certificates, they needed yet another one so many couldn't leave. In 1994, the so-called blue roads were opened, but we have very little time, and I'd rather not go into any detail of those developments. It would be too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the Serbs prevent civilians from leaving the town?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: No, never. They actually wanted to leave because their families, their relatives were in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did civilians get killed by sniper fire on the Serbian side of the city?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Especially in the part that was under the control of Serbian soldiers, in the part of Sarajevo which is known as Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did civilians get killed by other kind of fire in the Serbian part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: There was a case in October with UN observers. I went to the hospital where an 11-year-old girl was dying, helpless. She had lost both legs, and the doctors could not sedate her because there were no medicines and we all cried. So people died as a result of shelling. The doctors cried. I cried myself. My best man, who was a surgeon, said she would be gone in ten minutes. And that proved to be correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to make a break after the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ilidza had been shelled. That's when that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are again invited to make a break after the question before you start your answer. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not recorded what was shelled.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: The centre of Ilidza was shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D2798 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And before the document appears on the screen, could you please tell us whether any member of your family was killed or injured in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: My two uncles were killed. The first one in Grbavica, as a result of sniping from the Muslim side. He was a Croat, and he was on his way to fetch his retirement money cheque.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: His name was Milovan Markovic. And the case we have on the screen is the case of my other uncle, Marinko Vujicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. Let me ask you, you see the image on the screen. What does it depict?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: This is the exhumation of my uncle, Marinko Vujicic. He been killed in Dobrinja at the beginning of 1992. His body was exhumed with the help of Americans, sometime in 1998 or 1999, but I'm not sure of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D02799.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you know about the way your uncle, Marinko Vujicic, was killed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: My aunt, Milojka Vujicic told me that he had been taken away from their apartment. She said that members of some police force had arrived. She told me that he been tortured, that he had been detained. He was beaten up there. And after that, she never inquired about him. She didn't know anything about his fate. Only later did she learn that had he been killed and buried very close to their apartment, perhaps 400 metres away from their building in front of another building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is this another photo from the exhumation of your uncle?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I took the photo myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What does this photo depict?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: This photo depicts some broken bones.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let us look at 1D2797.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You see a man in a uniform. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the Green Berets of the American army. Those forces were in charge of special operations. I was their interpreter and translator and they were the one who is helped me with the exhumation. They secured the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who does the skull belong to?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: To my late uncle, Marinko Vujicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender all the three photos into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do object to the admission of the photos. The -- well, I haven't objected to the testimony coming in. The photos, as far as I can tell, are not relevant to the responsibility of the accused for the crimes charged in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The photos and the whole part of the testimony is very important to understand our rebuttal of the witnesses who testified here for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In what respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because they denied that there were any crimes. We had even the inspector, police inspector, who praised himself that he was this charge of war crimes in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I maintain the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now we will move on to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2798 receives number D520. Document 1D2799 receives number D521. And document 1D2797 receives number D522, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D520 up to and including D522 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may. However, could the parties at any point in time consider to agree on whether crimes were committed, whether snipers fired also at people living in the Serb-controlled areas of Sarajevo. I don't know whether you have ever discussed it, because we hear evidence that persons were killed by shelling. Now, is it the position of the Prosecution that shells never fell there or -- it's all rather vague and rather -- killed by a shell somewhere. But if the parties were in a position to agree on these matters, that would -- might save a lot of time, and I would suggest that you sit together and see what would or would not be possible in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I repeatedly stated throughout the trial, the Prosecution is willing to sit down and seriously consider any proposal from the Defence. Of course, we would want to be able to verify that the fact that we agree to is accurate. We wouldn't want the Chamber to include facts that are inaccurate simply because we agreed to them. So -- but we're happy to do that at any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, would that be a suggestion to give it a serious effort?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We will -- we have this task of making the statements first. And only when -- because everybody is submerged into this task, we all do -- are working on that part so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It saves a lot of time in taking statements to deal repetitiously with matters which might not be in dispute. So, therefore, an investment there could save time in the long-term. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Batinic, and now I will have a few questions about your military engagement. When were you mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: The classical mobilisation started on the 20th of June. My relatives and my neighbours and myself were taken to the line near Zenik. That would have been the classical mobilisation. But when it comes to the arming of the Territorial Defence to which we all belonged, that had taken place even before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is just an introduction I wanted to make to ask you how you became an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: I'll have to laugh a bit, Your Honours. I believe it's the only case that somebody became an interpreter in that way. On the 28th of June, that was my first combat experience defending a position, and my machine-gun broke down. The next day, I went to the Igman Brigade to have my machine-gun repaired because it had jammed in the middle of fighting. They repaired it for me, and the next day I went again to get ammunition so I can go back to my position. And while I was waiting for this logistics man, I was sitting outside and saw a truck arriving. I believe there were three observers and a girl with them, and I greeted them in English. They went in to see the commander while I continued to sit outside, and some half an hour later, the commander, whom I, by the way, didn't know at all, called me in and asked: Do you speak English? I said yes. And then he said: Okay. From now on, you'll be an interpreter. That's how I became an interpreter in the brigade. Can I explain a bit about what happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you see, the record says that you became an interpreter in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: That's what the commander said: From now on you'll be my interpreter. However, as I was working with Military Observers -- and I was even wearing my normal uniform at the time and none of the UNMOs told me that I am not supposed to wear that uniform. One day, a Danish man came in and said: How can you wear the VRS uniform when you are --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you're invited to slow down. Otherwise part of your words will be lost. We were at the point where you said: "One day, a Danish man came in and said: How can you wear the VRS uniform when --" and then, would you please resume from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll slow down. I'm just in a hurry because our time is short and there are so many things to say. So he said: How can you still wear a uniform when you are a UN interpreter? And I said: Well, nobody had told me this before. So I went to see the commander Blagota Kovacevic [phoen]. And the commander says: Well, if that's what they told you, then turn your uniform back in to supplies. And from that time on, I went around in civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I just put one question for clarification of the records to you. You were referring to the 28th and 29th of June. Which year are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for asking, Your Honour. That was year 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I also have a question for clarification. You told us that your commander called you in after you greeted some people in English. And said from then on you are going to be a commander -- you're going to be an interpreter for him. Now this was a VRS commander, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you please explain the transition from being an interpreter for the commander to being an interpreter for the UNMOs, because the two are now being mixed. I'm not quite sure when you became the interpreter for the UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll explain the details. On the 30th of June, I received an UNPROFOR ID card indicating I was an interpreter although not a qualified one. So I had on the Serb uniform with a UN ID card. That's where the confusion lay. Because nobody had told me at that point that I, as a UN interpreter, cannot be a uniformed person. But the commander had initially told me I would be his interpreter. I was an interpreter, actually, for both him and the UNMOs. And in July, a Dane arrived, who was better trained than the other observers, and he was the first one who told me: How can you wear a uniform? You are a civilian. You are a UN interpreter. So I went to see my commander, and he said: Well, in that case, take your uniform off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] I would now like to look at a video-clip. I gave the transcript in both B/C/S and English to the booths. The audio is rather bad, but I believe with the -- between the audio and the text we can understand it. We would rely on both the text and the audio. Could we play 1D02796. My colleague Mr. Ivetic will do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll a play it twice. Is it a long version?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's two and half minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two and a half minutes. Okay, we'll play it twice. The first round to verify the accuracy of the transcript, and then in the second round hear the translation, interpretation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see it the second time with the translation now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We play it again and we'd like to hear the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Today the medical personnel of the Blazuj hospital found two tanks with interesting contents among the oxygen tanks received as humanitarian aid. "The oxygen tanks were opened in the presence of UNPROFOR, and in one of them gunpowder was found while the other was filled with mortar fuses. "We are asking Dr. Pejic how did these tanks end up in the hospital. "Dr. Pejic: This is how they arrived. The police at the border crossing at Kobiljaca established that there were some oxygen tanks being transported to the Kosevo Hospital or somewhere else, and pursuant to some procedure, they took out ten tanks to be delivered to this area here. Out of those ten, this hospital got five. "To our astonishment, we found out that two of the five tanks did not contain oxygen, that they were much heavier than the others. "At first we thought it was water or something frozen, because the weather was so cold, but even when it got warmer the tanks were as heavy as before. And then we decided to call in the people who knew how to handle these things. "They opened the tanks and found out that they contained gunpowder. "Female reporter: We do not know how many shipments like this one have arrived in the hands of Muslim fighters through the UNPROFOR under the motto 'Humanity Without Borders,' and we do not know how many missiles have been made from their contents, do we? "But considering the fact that in the recent months all the Serb positions around Sarajevo, especially those at Hadzici and Ilidza, have been shelled with handmade missiles every day, killing many innocent civilians, especially children, we can say that with certainty a lot of such shipments have arrived."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you present -- we've heard and seen this video. On this occasion, were you present on the spot, at the scene?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was present at the scene. In fact, Dr. Pejic had called into the -- had called in UNMOs, and we were the first team who arrived there. We established already in the depot that they contained gunpowder, these tanks, and after that, members of the French Battalion were called in, along with French -- along with television crews. But in the first part, when the tanks were opened inside the depot, we were the only ones there, and I was the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You heard what Dr. Pejic said. Was it established that one tank contained mortar fuses and the other gunpowder?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes. We opened the first tank also, and a minute after we opened the tank, the gunpowder turned into some sort of emulsion, a gel-like substance, probably because of the contact with air.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would offer this video into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't object to the video but we need a little bit more clarification about its provenance, where does it come from, what's the -- broadcast from where. I don't think we even know the date of this incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will try to cover that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we put it on hold tendering it until we have heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.
