utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You heard what my learned friend Ms. Hasan wants to know. Do you know who made this footage? Do you know the time when this was happening? If you know.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: This was footage made by a local Serb television, after the report from Mr. Pejic -- Dr. Pejic. But I know that we arrived before the TV crew, and in the depot we opened one of the tanks. As for the time, I am certain it is 1992. The weather was rather cold, and looking at the image of this Danish reporter, with whom I spent some time together under shelling sometime later, I would guess it was October or November. I know I was wearing a blue jacket, and it was rather cold.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does this footage correspond to what you saw on the ground? I mean, does this reflect the same situation as when you were present.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking at it. I am looking at the transcript in order not to reply too fast. Yes, it's certainly that same footage. But after our first on-site investigation, the French -- the French Battalion arrived, and then the TV crew, and Dr. Pejic [Realtime transcript read in error "Dr. Karadzic"] was still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If the objection by the Prosecution still stands, I can ask for this video to be MFI'd, since Dr. Pejic will be here and he will testify about the same video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May be good reason to ask a number to be assigned and MFI the video. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2796 receives number D523, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D523 is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I say something about what is written here. The record says "Dr. Karadzic." No, it was Dr. Pejic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I see Dr. Pejic will be here but -- oh, further [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see "Dr. Karadzic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that the -- interpreter saying Dr. Pejic was still there. But the transcript will be reviewed after this hearing, Mr. Batinic, so it's appreciated that you offer your assistance --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I mean to say is I was never with Dr. Karadzic, and he wasn't there, at this place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has been clarified. Mr. Lukic, we'll take a break in five minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, we can move on to another topic and finish it quickly. Were you present at the transportation of people from one side of the confrontation line to the other by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the airport?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The airport.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very well. It was sometime in 1993, if I remember well. I was accompanying a Danish observer, Mr. Jan Pedersen, a member of an UNMO section. He also had the chief of Lima with him, a Russian observer, Sergei Fyodorov [phoen]. There was also a Swiss man recording the whole event on camera, on video camera, and I was there as an interpreter. I remember the Military Observers had received a report, and I was there interpreting, concerning some suspicious activity across the airport; namely, that French forces were transporting Muslim troops across the airport. That was a shocking report, and we went to have a look. It was at night-time. We went there, and we were perhaps 800 metres away from the runway on the side controlled by the VRS at a terrace of a house under cover, and we had a very good view of what was going on since there was no rain and the visibility was quite good. Under the headlights of the patrolling APCs, you could see that a part of -- that Muslim soldiers were boarding French APCs, about ten men per vehicle, and then they were moved to the other side. The members of the patrols were not involved, only one part of them were involved, those closer to Dobrinja. It was a shock to us. It was all recorded and it was all turned over to the UNPROFOR staff but we never saw that footage. It was never published. It seems to have vanished. And from what Jan and Sergei said, they called it "French taxi." So, for money, the French soldiers, the French UNPROFOR, gave a lift to the enemy side. A month later, the tunnel was opened so there was no need for that service anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Time for a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes, Mr. Batinic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at 20 minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted back into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I put on the record that the original of the papers that the witness provided to the Chamber have been returned to him during the last break. Mr. Mladic wants to consult apparently. Mr. Stojanovic, first thing you should tell him is that he can remain seated. Please be seated, Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Mladic wants to address Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, he needs -- if he wants to address the Chamber, Mr. Lukic, you know what it is. You can ask permission, identifying exactly what Mr. Mladic intends to do, but it's not just standing up and claiming that he can address the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We -- Mr. Mladic wanted us to raise the same issue and I wanted to finish with this witness, thinking that we had enough fuss today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He wants to address the Chamber regarding his health, that he cannot follow the trial for five days a week, that he really feels sick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then what should be done is that you file again or make any submissions to express that, and it's also a matter which should not be delayed too much. Therefore, if you would need time, you can make submissions tomorrow morning, and -- so that we hear about it without delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And we, you know, instructed Mr. Mladic to tell the doctor who is coming this afternoon the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Well, you don't -- the Chamber is not -- whatever Mr. Mladic thinks that he should tell the doctor, he should tell the doctor. That is with or without instructions. And certainly the Chamber stays out of it. The Chamber will receive later a report, and we'll carefully consider whatever is written in that report. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Batinic, can we continue?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. Mr. Mladic, you should not inappropriately seek contact in any way with the public gallery. This is where it happens, not in the public gallery, so refrain from such actions. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Batinic, do you remember that you interpreted something at a meeting concerning incidents in May 1992, known as the breadline incident in Vase Miskina. Could you tell us briefly about that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember interpretation in relation to that incident that had happened in the past. I wasn't working as an interpreter at the time. However, I remember a meeting - it was sometime in the beginning of 1993 - that had to do with this topic. It was in the Igman Brigade. The commander was lieutenant-colonel at the time, Spasoje Cojic. He is an artillery man otherwise. And I think that UNMOs were being made aware of this, and then the team was still in the brigade, and we often talked. I was present at the only interpreter for at that team. At that time the team was called Lima 2. Later on it changed its name to Sierra Whiskey 1. I remember that Commander Cojic explained that it is the Serb side that is always blamed for everything. And then, as an artillery expert, he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I interrupt for a second. The question was about a meeting concerning incidents in May 1992. You're now telling us about the beginning of 1993. Is -- I'm just seeking clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I incident was in May 1992. And that incident from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the meeting was in the beginning of 1993? Is that ... yes, that's what the witness said. This clarifies the issue. Yes. In the -- in the English translation, it's unclear whether May 1992 refers to the incidents or to the meeting. That's -- that's what I sought to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, continue, where you were interrupted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I shall proceed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can barely hear the witness. Could he please be asked to speak into the microphone, and could all unnecessary microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please come closer to the microphone. The interpreters have difficulties hearing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me better now? So, in 1993, actually, it was the time when the brigade commander, Cojic, got to meet the Military Observers and this was an extensive meeting dealing with different topics, and, in a way, this was touched upon too. Namely, that the Serbs were always Satanised by the media. And then Commander Cojic mentioned, as an example, that incident from 1992, May, it was towards the end of May 1992. It was called the breadline incident. It was televised at the time. It was an incident when many civilians got killed in this bread line. And I know full well that he explained that it wasn't the Serb forces that had caused this incident. Rather, that it had been staged. He explained this by saying the following. No projectile was ever fired at the bread line. Rather, in this narrow street, Vase Miskina, there were land-mines that were in cellars of buildings in this street. Also, according to the pathology reports, there was a statement of the body parts that were injured, and on the basis of that, he said with 100 per cent certainty that this was not a mortar shell. Rather, that the whole incident had been staged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The people that you interpreted for, did they object, or did they agree, or did they simply take no position?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, these people had no position whatsoever. They listened carefully because they are officers too. Now, what part of the military they belonged to, I really don't know. But, quite simply, they listened to that, surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move onto a different topic. The content is similar. The Markale incident on the 5th of February, 1994. As an interpreter, did you participate in this meeting that had to do with this incident? Can you tell us who the participants were and when this took place?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: I remember very well. Again, this Jan Pedersen was on the team. He is a Dane. This was 1994, February. On his Motorola, he heard from UN headquarters in Sarajevo that they were asking for an urgent investigation regarding this incident. So we tried to establish direct contact with General Stanislav Galic, who was commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. First we went to the Igman Brigade in order to establish contact to see where the general was and then we heard that the general was attending a meeting in Ilidza that was under Serb control. We got into a vehicle and we went to Hotel Serbia, as it was called at the time, where the general had a meeting. However, we did not have an opportunity to contact the general, who was attending a meeting. However, his security man, if I can call him that, came to speak to us, Colonel Marko Lugonja. When speaking to Marko, when we told him what happened, I noticed that then-Colonel Lugonja was quite simply astonished. His comment was: Well, that's impossible. He said: The Serb side did not do this. Well, we're not stupid to do that because, as he said, there are some negotiations going on right now, somewhere abroad. But at any rate, come back in an hour to headquarters, to my headquarters in Lukavica, and I am going to give you all the necessary information. I will check what it was that happened. I'm going to check through my security service and see what it was that had happened. After an hour or so, I and Jan went to Colonel Lugonja, who, in a way, was standing in for Galic as his first officer, and he said: Please, take a seat. I know what happened. We sat there in his office, and he immediately took a remote control, turned on the TV and -- actually, he was showing us a video on TV. And he said: Now I'm going explain this to you and please take a look at this carefully. My service already had this recorded, and they explained what happened. So as we were viewing this, he said: Pay attention to what is happening here. Take a look at these two men who are running away from the scene. This is suspicious. Please take a look at this. There is some plastic leg here. How come that is there? There is no body there. And then he said: Take a look at this. Look at these pyramids of potatoes that are on the stalls. This is a marketplace, right. Not a single potato had fallen. Look at the bottles that on stalls. Not a single bottle fell, not a single bottle was broken. Then, one thing can I tell you for sure, our intelligence service during this incident or before the incident found out that over the past seven days, from the mortuary Kosevo, no funerals were taking place. The bodies were kept at the mortuary there. Then our service intercepted a conversation between two ambulance drivers on the Muslim side and it can be heard quite clearly when one of them is telling the other in coded language: Bring me more icicles. I'm not a military expert I'm not an artillery man, that is what he said, but this is an enormous number of casualties if it's just a mortar shell. Also there are many people who are wounded and I really doubt that we were the ones who did that. It is not in our interest at all. I am convinced that this is rigged, a rigged process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The last sentence I would like to clarify. You said: "I am convinced that this is rigged, a rigged process." Is that your opinion or are you referring to the participant of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no opinion here. I am just interpreting simultaneously what Colonel Lugonja was saying, so I'm referring to his words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us exactly what day and what time this conversation, this meeting, took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the exact date. So as for the date when this incident happened, Markale, well, that's when it happened. And I and the UNMO heard about it via Motorola. He had contact with UN headquarters; that is to say, the information came from UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it was on the day of the incident itself, which, I think the parties would agree, is the 5th of February, 1994. What time exactly when you were watching this television, this video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was already after 12.00 when we were watching this. Perhaps two or three hours after the incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're done with that. Now I'm going to ask you -- actually, we're going to move on to the time when members of UNPROFOR were being taken prisoner after the NATO bombing of Serb positions started. Could you please tell us whether - and in which way - you took part in observing the situation.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are talking about the year 1995. I don't know whether it was in spring or in summer. I was a member of the Sierra Whiskey team. I was their interpreter. Olivier Mrowicki was the team leader. He was an air force man.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Do you know the -- that name was misspelled. Could you please slowly tell us the name of that man.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: He was a French captain at the time. He was an air force member. Olivier Mrowicki with a W.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please look at the screen and see whether this has been spelled properly.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: No. Olivier is correct but it is not Murowitski. Let me spell in the military way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you do that again in the military way but a bit slower.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be my honour, Your Honours. I'm looking at the name Olivier is correct. And now M-r-o-w-i-c-k-i.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you have a look at the screen whether it's now correctly spelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under A, I can't see anything and there's nothing below that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, do you see page 59, line 14?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: The -- the typing is going on, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the typing is going on. If you move on eight lines, there you find a word spelled. Otherwise, the usher should assist you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not correct. Yeah, that's correct. That's correct now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And we mentioned Olivier Mrowicki and then I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Olivier Mrowicki was the team leader and his deputy was Captain Andy, a Brit, I can't remember his last name. We were in the sector of the Igman Brigade after the bombing. Commander Cojic assigned a guard to join the team. The team was billeted in the former cafe Mediterrane [phoen]. And in my conversation with the commander, I told him that I guaranteed that there would be no problem, that people would not flee, that I would be there all the time because I lived there and so on and so forth. And that's how things transpired. There were no problems at all, the observers were semi-free, I have to say. Their movement was limited to the house and the area around the house. There was also a guard there. That guard had an automatic rifle. However, as days went by, the rifle would be left in the room and while the guard was outside of the house, which means that that rifle was accessible to everybody who wanted to get a hold of it. And the observers enjoyed good treatment. I remember well that together with Captain Mrowicki, we boarded my vehicle to go to Ilidza. We didn't want to use an UNPROFOR vehicle in order to avoid attention. The commander of the 1st Battalion, Sesa, even gave him a Serb uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the name Sesa [Realtime transcript read in error "Seselj"]. Do you know his name?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: His name is Svetozar Guzina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said: "You mentioned the name Sesa." And instead of "Sesa" I read "Seselj." The name should be corrected. It's good now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, whenever you see such a little sign it means that it will be verified after this hearing because there are doubts already on the accuracy of spelling. There's no need to have it corrected on the spot. Otherwise, sessions would take two hours longer a day. Could I seek clarification? Witness, you said they were semi-free, although they were limited in their movement. Limited to the house and to the area around the house. And then -- first of all, do I understand they were not allowed to leave and go back to the units, would they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. When I said that they were semi-free, I meant that their movement was restricted. They were not allowed to leave the territory. They could be in the house and around the house. They were not tied. They were not forced to do anything. They were not taken away. There was a guard there, but they were on really good terms with that guard. They even shared drinks together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then -- this is the type of semi-freedom every prisoner has, isn't it? He can stand up in his cell, he can walk in his cell. Even during a couple of hours, he may be outside in the yard. Is that what you consider to be semi-freedom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let me put my next question to you, which is, you said: Well, the guard was outside the house, and his rifle was accessible to everyone. You seem to suggest that those who were not free to leave could have taken that gun and could have used it and -- and that was all without -- they were free to do all that and nothing would happen to them. That's the suggestion in your answer. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we did not understand each other. I'd like to put this whole thing in simpler terms, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I thought there might be some misunderstanding. That's the reason why I'm seeking clarification. What about access to the rifle? Would you really consider it an option for them to go to that rifle and to use it and then take that rifle and walk out? Is that your suggestion? If not, please tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me simplify. The Military Observers had their own rooms. They were not confined to a classical prison. The guard who was assigned to watch them carried that weapon only one day. Already on the following day he left his weapon in the room while he went to the toilet or while he decided to leave the room, which means that the observers were free in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So they could take that weapon and walk out? Is that your suggestion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They could but they did not. It didn't even cross their mind. Because they knew that nothing would happen to them, judging by the way that they were treated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But they couldn't leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me give you an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Their movement was restricted but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So they were not too free to leave. That's -- if I understood you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You understood me well. That's correct. However, Olivier Mrowicki --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We've heard the other details you've told us. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue. You started by saying "Oliver Mrowicki," who did what at that moment?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Since we were good friends and since we both knew the commander, Svetozar Guzina, we went to his place for a drink and he told him: My friend, I'm giving you a uniform. Put it on so nobody will provoke you, so nobody will take you for an observer, and -- and Lola can take you anywhere you want to go. And we did go to places. I took him to Vogosca. There were telephone lines there so he could talk to his family. And then we returned to the team. We went shopping for food, fruit juices. One day, we even went across Sierra 1, which was the check-point of the Serbian army and police, in the direction of Kiseljak, which means that he left the territory, in legal terms, which was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska. Then he put a French uniform on and the security guy who was at the check-point who knew me gave me two hours. I told him we had to go and fetch food and fuel, and the security guy told me: Lola, you have two hours, you have to be back within two hours. I'm holding you responsible, you have to come back within two hours. We went in the direction of Kiseljak. We crossed the Serbian check-point, and then we were stopped by Canadians, who were taken by surprise. They thought that we were headed for the Serbian side. They never realised that we had arrived from the Serbian side, and then they directed us towards Kiseljak, and then Mrowicki played dumb and he said: Thank you for directing us in that way. We wouldn't know where to go otherwise and we were on our way to fetch food and fuel anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the whole introduction of this was episode was a bit unclear to me. Was that French person alone in that house? I mean, the description is not very clear. And I do understand that he was confined to that house, but he could go with you wherever he wanted to go but he should return. Well, it's -- it's entirely unclear to me, if you read or re-read the beginning of this episode, then there is no framework in which I can put that. So if you would please do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, was Mrowicki also a prisoner in that house?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: That was not a prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So who -- what was his position?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: He was the head of the Sierra Whiskey 1 team, and the team members were all in that house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then my next question would be, Mr. Lukic: Were these other team members also taken out for shopping or for filling up their cars with gasoline, or did they stay behind in this semi-freedom on those premises?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the other observers did not go anywhere with us. They were in the house or around the house. They could not go shopping. I gave my word to Commander Cojic for Mrowicki. I vouched for his safety with my life. I was grateful to UNPROFOR, they saved my life in 1994, and it was my duty to repay that service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you ever considered that Mrowicki felt unsafe not to return when all the others were still in semi-freedom on those premises? Have you considered that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it never crossed my mind. I trusted Mrowicki.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us see. You went to Kiseljak. You arrived there after you were instructed by Canadians how to get there and then you returned to the house where the others were.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was some two hours after we purchased the food and gasoline. But then we faced the problem with the same Canadians. We didn't know how to return to the Serbian territory. It was a mission impossible. We went across Lepenica, there's a little road that I knew from before the war, so that's how -- the road that we took to go back. And then we laughed at how we outsmarted the Canadians because there are rules in the war, and one of them is to be resourceful and see how to get by.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I must say that Judge Orie understood you better than I did. I never realised that Mrowicki was in the same group as the other observers but Judge Orie helped me to understand. Now I would like to know this: In the house where they were billeted, had they been brought there or was there a place where they were normally billeted even before their freedom of movement was restricted?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: They were in that house. The commander arrived with that soldier. We talked, and that's where they stayed. And the commander said, I remember what he said: I will have a different treatment to -- towards you. Please trust me. Don't provoke me in any way because nothing happen to you. I'm restricting your freedom of movement but I also guarantee you safety. I believe that that guard was there not to guard them but rather to protect them from the locals.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that we're done with that topic as well. And now, just briefly, I'd like to go back to the times preceding the war. Before the war, what did you know about Muslim paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: As early as in 1991, there were rumours. There were always rumours about some organisations known as the Green Berets, the Patriotic League. The war had already been on in Croatia. Ethnically based parties had already been established. Ethnic groups were firmly tied to their leaders and the staple topic was who was to blame. And then we heard about the Green Berets as a group of armed people, but there was no accurate information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was their first action in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: From what I remember, the first action was the killing of a member of a Serb wedding party. I believe it was in March 1992. And that spread panic among the Serbs. People were asking what happened in town. At that time we heard it was done by members of the Green Berets. I believe the name of one man was Baranovic. He was taken into custody, taken to the police station but very quickly released, so the Serbs stopped believing in the justice system. It was obvious that he was the killer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, thank you. Those were all the questions I had for you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Ms. Hasan, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Hasan. Ms. Hasan is counsel for the Prosecution. You find her to your right.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This is a honour for me, Ms. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could I just, for the record, get you to state your name. I just noticed we don't have that.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: My name is Milorad, last name Batinic. My nickname is Lola.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was on the record, Ms. Hasan, but I'm just trying to find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sorry, I may have missed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Batinic, I'm just going to go back to the statements that were taken, or the statement that was taken, from you. Now, you mentioned that you went to Pale together with the Defence team member, Mr. Dundjer.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Where did you go in Pale?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: We took the new road which goes across Trebevic because he was in a hurry and that's a shortcut. So we arrived at the centre of Pale. We met up there in a cafe facing the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you drove Mr. Dundjer to -- to that cafe. Did you stay with him throughout his meeting with the three other witnesses that you recall having been there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was there with him, and I was at that cafe.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And that's where you mentioned you saw Mr. Zdravko Cvoro; is that right? Cvoro.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: That's right. I remember Cvoro. I don't know about Zdravko, but I remember Cvoro. It's also the name of a journalist I know, and that's how I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Did you speak to Mr. Cvoro in Pale?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it speaking. We were just introduced. I shook his hand, saying: I think I know you from somewhere, and the rest of the conversation was done by Mr. Dundjer.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Did you hear Mr. Dundjer discuss the evidence of Mr. Cvoro with him during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: I don't know what they were discussing concerning the statement. The point was to have the document signed. I don't think there was much conversation. Mr. Cvoro had his statement before him. There was more talk about the schedule of departures to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about a few other individuals, and I'd like you to tell me in you saw these individuals either in Belgrade or in Pale, and for each individual, if you did see them, can you specify whether it was in Belgrade or Pale. Mile Sladoje?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Is that Commander Sladoje?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Again, I'm not sure it's the same man, but I think I met him in East Sarajevo, on that same day, when we went to Pale. I'm not sure if that's the same Sladoje. I know another commander, Cedo Sladoje. But if you show me the picture, I'll remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. And did you have any discussions with Mile Sladoje?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: I don't know what we would have to talk about.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about what you would have to talk about. Did you have a conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Please. If you have a photograph, I'll remember which Sladoje it is, because it's such a common surname. I don't want to make a mistake. If you show me a photo, I'll remember everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Let's try it this way. The Sladoje that you saw there, did you have any discussions with that person?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: If that's the same Sladoje, I believe I saw him. But I'm telling you, I don't know which one of the two it was. Two years ago, I even attended a funeral of one Sladoje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, did you see more than one Sladoje when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tell us whether you had a conversation with him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I talked to one Sladoje at the cafe, while the others were over there, signing statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So you have a conversation. What was the subject of your conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that's the same Sladoje --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- if we're talking about the same person, I asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are not talking about -- I am talking exclusively about the Sladoje you have seen there. You don't have to bother about whether -- what Sladoje I have on my mind. I haven't told you yet. Just talk about the Sladoje you saw there and tell us what the subject of your conversation was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked him, because the face was familiar, and if that's that same Sladoje that was the commander of security somewhere --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you not to bother about whether he is the same or a different one. I asked you about your conversation with that person you say had the name Sladoje. What was the subject of your conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we know each other, more or less, all of us, and it's a very common name, I asked him what he was doing during the war. He said he was in the security. Then I asked him: Do you know this man, or that man. But I personally didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Just so you know, Witness, I'm going to read the names of other individuals who signed declarations similar to you on the dates that you were in Pale. So I'd like to ask you then about Mr. Stevan Veljevic. Was he present; and, if so, where?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: I don't remember this Veljevic. He wasn't at all interesting to me. Can I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Ms. Hasan is just trying to find out whether some persons were present and whether you remember them when you went to the place where you signed your statement and later to Pale. Carefully listen to the questions and answer them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, just to clarify this. You say you don't remember this Veljevic. "He was not at all interesting to me." How do you know that he was not interesting to you if you don't remember him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when some names from our region are mentioned, because we are a small country and I'm a historian, when you mention a surname, the Google in my brain starts working. I know some routes, I know where names come from, which area. But when this Veljevic was mentioned, it didn't ring a bell. I didn't make a connection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. What you are saying is: I have no recollection that any of the persons who were there was known to you by the name of Veljevic. If that's your answer, then that's clear. Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Now it's clear to me too.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: All right. What about Milorad Dzida?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: I don't know about him. I've never seen him. Maybe he was there. I only paid attention to this Cvoro because of the famous anchorwoman named Cvoro. And I asked him about his family, where he is from, because this woman is -- is very beautiful, and I thought perhaps it's his daughter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, could you please briefly answer the questions. Ms. Hasan will now mention other names and what she wants to know is whether there was any person there which you knew by that name. Nothing more, nothing less, whether they had beautiful daughters or parents. Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So let's move on to the next person. Slavko Gengo.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes. Slavko Gengo. That's, in fact, the name whose name I confused. That's the person I sat in the cafe with. I was sitting with Slavko, and we discussed my brother-in-law, a Croat, who was with him in the barracks before the war. Now it's coming back to me. Forget about that first person. The one who sat with me in the cafe is Gengo.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sorry, you say "forget about the first person." Which person are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the one --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sladoje. Forget about Sladoje. Gengo is the one who was with me in the cafe.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, with -- with your discussions with Mr. Gengo in the cafe, besides talking to him about his -- about your brother-in-law, did you discuss any of the information in your statement or any information in his statement or -- or your upcoming testimony here?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we didn't discuss anything. We didn't discuss any statements whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Dragan Maletic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: The name is familiar, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Is it familiar because you saw him that day?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Possibly. Very possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Nikola Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: The name is familiar. I may have seen him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: You may have seen him. Do you -- do you recall having any discussions with him on that specific day?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: If I see a photograph, I might remember. From the name, I can't tell you anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Zdravko Cvoro. Oh, sorry, we already discussed him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've dealt with him, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Predrag Trapara.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Trapara is a very large family, a common name. I don't know if it's the same person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, again, the simple question is whether there was any person present known to you by the name mentioned by Ms. Hasan. Was there anyone that was known to you as bearing the name Trapara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember. I don't remember that person.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have three more names to go through. I notice it's the break time but we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if the witness would limit his answer to what is asked, then I think we could finish that part and you'll continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So if could you be brief. Branko Radan, was he there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Veljko Lubura.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Dusan Skrba.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we turn into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you are certain about the -- let's move into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The usher could already prepare for the witness to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We'll take a break. The witness will be escorted out of the courtroom by the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we'll resume at a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, I deal with the Defence request for leave to reply. Such a request was filed on the 15th of May of this year. It was a request for leave to file a reply to the Prosecution's response to the Defence's Rule 92 ter motion pertaining to Witness GRM258. The Chamber hereby grants the request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, meanwhile, I also deal with another matter -- yes, the witness is there, so I'll refrain from continuing with any other matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, I'd like you to take a look at the signature page that you signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 30799.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you see it on your screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing appears on our screens at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, let me just proceed and ask you: After --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's there now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we see the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, now, after you were -- when you were given your statement that day and you carefully reviewed it, did you go through and count the number of pages of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've read -- I read it, and I counted the pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And was it you who filled that in and wrote nine pages there. That's your writing?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: As for the number nine, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can we take a look at 65 ter 30798.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, this is what I think is the first statement, the statement that you actually reviewed. I just want to flip through it and ensure that, in fact, this is the one that you reviewed and signed off on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we could just turn to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, are you able to confirm that that was the statement that you reviewed? If you need more time to look at it, I can get a hard copy for you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: No need for that. It's the 2nd of May, 2014. 25 paragraphs. As far as I can remember, I signed 27 paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the 27-paragraph statement is not nine pages. It's six pages. So this one is nine pages so -- Ms. Hasan, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if you signed a nine page and if you verified that, couldn't be the 27-paragraph statement because that's shorter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have that statement, unsigned, in my room, and I will gladly give it to you. It hasn't been signed. It has 27 paragraphs, so I don't understand this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Neither do I at this moment. Madam Registrar, is there a possibility that the Victims and Witness Section would accompany the witness to his hotel room after the end of this court session and receive from him the statement he says he has in his hotel room. And that's the copy he received when signing but the extra copy that he took home and which he had at home and which he used for further preparing his comments to be given in The Hague. That is a request to that -- that the Victims and Witness Section will accompany you. The parties cannot do that, Witness, because they're not allowed to have contact with you once you have taken the stand. Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, when you met with Mr. Dundjer to review your statement, you have already told us that you -- there were some corrections you wanted to make. Now, did you inform Mr. Dundjer what those corrections were at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: There were mistakes in terms of years, names, and I said: I won't sign this. And then Dundjer said pressure coming from The Hague to get this done. I will do all the corrections with Lukic, and I only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you've told us that already three times. Just focus on the question put to you by Ms. Hasan, whether you informed Mr. Dundjer at the time what the changes were you wanted to make. Apparently you did. It is about dates and names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And did you see Mr. Dundjer take notes of those corrections?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, did you, subsequent to your meeting with Mr. Dundjer, or before that, meet with a Sasa Lukic to discuss the information you were to provide in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Did you meet with someone by the name of Boris Zorko [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes. But not last time. Before that. I don't know exactly when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, there may be some ambiguity in your question as far as timing is concerned. Witness, did you ever meet or were you ever interviewed by a person by the name of Sasa Lukic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think that was last year. In eastern Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. And just in regard to Boris Zorko, you said you met with him very briefly. Did he interview you about your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Boris Zorko was with Sasa Lukic. Last year we were in contact in eastern Sarajevo, sometime in the autumn.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue there, were you then interviewed by Zorko and Lukic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last year? No. Except in March last year. That was the first meeting. Then I gave some statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Why did you then meet them or were you in contact with him in autumn -- in the autumn of last year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is when they came to eastern Sarajevo in relation to witness-related questions. I gave them some other contacts so that they could contact some other people in respect of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us whose names you then gave to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vojislav Carkic, a priest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And apart from him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall any others. I don't think I mentioned anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you said, "I gave them some other contacts so they could contact some other people." You're not saying: I gave them one other contact so that they could contact one other person. But you were talking in the plural, and I'm asking you who else you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour. I mentioned Lieutenant-Colonel Sergei Fyodorov from Moscow. What kind of contacts were established with this person and whether that actually happened, I don't know. That's why I said that in the plural. This had to do with eastern Sarajevo, and that's why I mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now a minute ago you said: "I don't recall any others." And when I insisted, you immediately came with another person. Any explanation for not knowing any others and half a minute later to come with another name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely because I focussed on eastern Sarajevo, Your Honour. And Priest Vojislav Carkic stayed on with Lukic and they talked, and this person has many more contacts. I remembered the other name when you mentioned the plural, then I remembered Sergei. But he is not in eastern Sarajevo, he is in Moscow. He is in Russia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would please focus on the question as put to you instead of developing your own framework of thought when answering questions. Just listen to the question and answer them. Please proceed, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, at this interview that Mr. Lukic, Sasa Lukic, and Boris Zorko conducted, was Milenko Dundjer present?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether Mr. Boris or Mr. Dundjer were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If I understand your evidence correctly, you, on one occasion, meet with Sasa Lukic who interviews you and, on another occasion, Mr. Milenko Dundjer also interviews you. Do I have that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Let's deal with this chronologically then. March last year, I met Lukic, Sasa, and Boris, in Belgrade. After that, last autumn, Sasa came. I think he was on his own. And then this other time, there was Zorko and Dundjer. Because I drove them from the bus station to the hotel in eastern Sarajevo. The last contact was precisely Milenko Dundjer. That's the document that we talked about. Dundjer was on his own.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Did you meet with any of these three individuals again in April of 2013? So a month after your initial interview?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you make it two weeks, Ms. Hasan, I have the 26th of March --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and the 8th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can just confirm that the last contact was with Milenko Dundjer when I signed this document, this statement, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have not listened to the question. You referred to your interview in March 2013. Now, on the front page, it says that you were also interviewed on the 8th of April, 2013. That's over a year ago. Who was there in this interview two weeks after your March interview which you said took place in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just remember Belgrade, that April -- actually, no, I don't remember 2013.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you interviewed twice in the beginning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was interviewed in Belgrade. And the next one was this statement, the one that I signed here with Dundjer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, perhaps you should take the witness back to the front page of his -- which he signed. Could we have a look at --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That was 65 ter 30799.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at that. Witness, could you have a look with me, 26th of March, 2013, 8th of April, 2013, are recorded as you being interviewed. About the first one, you told us that was in Belgrade. The 8th of April, 2013, could you tell us where that interview took place and who interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I see here -- well, I just know that one signature was on the 26th of March, 2013. I don't know about these other dates. The last signed document is where the date is the 14th -- no, the 10th of October, 2014 [as interpreted]. I don't know about the rest, except for the first date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't see any October. What I see at this moment is an interview on the 26th of March, 2013, which you confirmed had taken place in Belgrade. You're telling us that you were not interviewed or you have no recollection of being interviewed on the 8th of April of last year? You're nodding no, so that is a negative answer. Then the 14th and the 16th, or the 14th to the 16th of February of this year, were you then interviewed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, what then remains is the date on which you signed this document, which was either the 10th of April or perhaps even the 10th of May. Now, you said on the 26th you were interviewed by whom exactly? By Sasa Lukic? I'm talking about March 2013, in Belgrade. Who were present there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sasa Lukic and Boris.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you were never interviewed by Milenko Dundjer on any of these dates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour. I had no conversation with him, just the signing of this statement that had already been printed out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And, Witness, just at line 14, page 84 of today's transcript, you say that on the 26th of -- on the 26th of March, 2013, that's -- you say: "I just know that I had -- one signature was on the 26th of March, 2013." Did you sign a statement on that date?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: I think I signed one. That was last year. I mean, I signed it. If my signature is there, then I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of that statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: I never got that copy, and I never took it either.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask that the Defence provide us with copy of the statement signed by the witness on that date so that we can review it this evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can tell that you no -- not a single statement was signed at that time. I can vouch for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has a statement been taken and put on paper on that date, irrespective of whether it was signed or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All I have -- and you know about the confusion. I can check with the office. But even if it is, then it's a work product and we did not get from the Prosecution those work products. But I will inquire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the line between what is work product and what is a statement, and of course the Prosecution is under an obligation to disclose any statement ever taken by a witness. And, Mr. Lukic, under the present circumstances, there may be some concern about what is statement and what is not. Yes, please proceed, Ms. Hasan, for the next two minutes because we have to adjourn timely today.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So, Witness, on the 10th of June, you met with Mr. Lukic to, as you say, make some corrections to your statement, the statement you had with you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This year, you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, the witness talked about Monday. Now Monday was the 9th of June. I don't know whether --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: It's the 9th of June that you met with Mr. Lukic and I received a note about the corrections on the 10th. So, Witness, do you recall that on the 9th of June, meeting with Mr. Lukic to discuss the corrections you made? You wanted to make?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's what I've said, that's what Mr. Lukic did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, you said you reviewed a document which recorded those corrections. The corrections made on that document, was -- were those the entire corrections that you made to your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BATINIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic corrected everything. However, this document was not received here. I'm sorry, may I just add something? That is why yesterday we opted for this other version in vivo. That is to say, that document had been rejected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You gave your corrections to Mr. Lukic. Now, did he incorporate them in your original statement, or did he make a separate document which contains the changes you had made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Lukic made the corrections. What happened further on, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I want to know, you said he immediately then produced the corrected statement. Did he -- or if you didn't see it, please tell us. Did he then have a separate document saying: This is a change, this is a change, this is a change? Or did he produce your original statement with the changes incorporated in that statement in its entirety? Which of the two? If you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think, Your Honour, that Mr. Lukic will explain that better. He is the one who made the corrections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you seen the document containing the corrections? Because, if not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, he typed that up, these corrections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that one page? Or was that, again, six, seven pages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was several pages. I sat on the balcony smoking as he was working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. We leave it to that. We'll adjourn for the day. Mr. Groome, we have to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just asking that the witness be given the standard admonition about not to speak to other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course I will. And now, first of all, Witness, once you leave the courtroom, you will be accompanied by the Victims and Witness Section to go to your hotel and to fetch whatever statements you still have. At least provide them all but certainly the one which was given to you on -- in Sarajevo when you signed a copy of your statement. Second, I would like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, and this is a very serious instruction, not by phone, not in any other way, do not speak with anyone or communicate with anyone about your testimony, whether given today or still to be given tomorrow or the coming days. If that's clear, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I take note of everything, and I do apologise if I was a bit emotional. All of this is something new to me. I wish you all a good day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
